title: Admissions as a compression algorithm
author: Doan Winkel
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), October 23, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel reacts to a LinkedIn post calling college admissions a leverage point for unwinding industrial-era schooling, and he prompts Claude to explore the question without limits. The long body of the post is Claude's answer, reproduced under Winkel's framing. It argues that admissions compresses years of a student into a few lossy proxies (GPA, tests, essay, activities) and that schools teach to the codec. Because AI has collapsed the cost of reading a rich record, the constraint that justified compression no longer binds, while AI has also killed the essay as a trustworthy signal. After reviewing four current retreats, the essay proposes a Defended Record: a portable record of process work, calibrated adult witnesses, and an oral defense of a year-long project before a panel that includes college faculty, followed by threshold, match, and lottery allocation. It names failure modes openly and notes that admitting on mastery forces colleges to teach on mastery. Readers should note the text is AI-generated and its statistics are unverified.
points: The central diagnosis is that admissions asks for claims about work and snapshots in time, which pushes high schools toward grades and polished narratives rather than curiosity.
The Defended Record would assess process (drafts, feedback, revisions) and a live oral defense, which makes AI use visible and hard to fake.
Calibrated witnesses would make recommenders accountable by scoring their predictions against later outcomes.
Separating readiness (a threshold) from allocation (match plus lottery) is meant to drive the return on endless polish to zero.
The essay concedes that colleges would have to change how they teach, since admitting on mastery while grading on curves would teach students to game the new system.
quotes: Start with what an admissions office actually is. It is a device for compressing three or four years of a human being into something a reader can evaluate in eight minutes. GPA is lossy compression of coursework.

The one true thing about 2026 is that the cost of reading a rich record just collapsed. A capable model can read a three-year portfolio of drafts and revisions, cross-reference it against a transcript, flag inconsistencies, and brief a human reader on what to probe in a conversation.
Almost everything in an application is an assertion about the student rather than an artifact by the student. The transcript asserts that learning happened. The rec asserts character.

A record that shows a student prompting a model, getting a draft, tearing it apart, and rebuilding it is a record of someone who can think with tools. A record that shows a finished essay appearing fully formed at 11:47 pm is a record of something else.
The defense is the AI-proof, consultant-proof, polish-proof layer, because the only way to do well in it is to have done the work and understood it.

If you admit on mastery, you have to teach on mastery, or the admissions system becomes a hypocrisy that students will decode in weeks. The faculty member who sat on the defense panel in March cannot hand that same student a scantron in September without feeling it.
The goal is not better sorting. Sorting is the industrial-era frame, and a more accurate sorting machine is still a sorting machine.
